abilities.text: Improved unit movement speed over an extended period.

abilities.text: Increases the effectiveness of the unit's charge for an extended period.

short: Exploratores translates as «scouts». In the inscriptions exploratores are connected with numeri and are divided into two kinds: exploratores et numerus, and numerus exploratorum. In this regard, there are two views in historiography defining their interrelation. Kallis, Mann, and Rowell consider exploratores and numerus to be two different units, while Stein, Nesselhauf, Watts, and Wiegels include both numerus and exploratores in the same category. It is known that there was a so-called «scout wreath» - corona exploratoria. It was given for successful scouting and was decorated with a stylized sun, moon and star. The main task of the exploratores, whose number, as far as we can judge, amounted to several dozen people was to discover the exact location or movement of the enemy forces and to collect data about the terrain. From Pseudo-Hyginus (2nd century) it follows that there were 200 exploratores for 3 legions (De munit. castr. 30). In addition, it was their duty to find out exactly the route that the main forces should follow, as well as to find a camp site (Caes. VS 11.17). The exploratores were not a separate independent unit until the Principate.
history: The supreme generals of the Roman Empire during 4th and 5th centuries AD were given the title ‘Magister Militum’. It was a prestigious position, that, when awarded to a particularly shrewd or political animal, held power rivalling, and sometimes outstripping, even that of the Emperor. Originally created during the reforms of Constantine the Great the title initially covered two specific positions, the Magister Equitum, ‘Master of the Horse’ and Magister Peditum, ‘Master of the Foot’. Over the years these roles merged, with generals who held both titles simply referred to as Magister Militum, ‘Master of Soldiers’. Separate Magister Militums were installed within each Roman territory. The great irony, when viewed in hindsight, is that the position was originally created by Constantine to rob one particular political foe of power, the usually-treacherous Prefect of the Praetorian Guard. However, those who held it generally became the bane of the Emperors they claimed to serve or, as on numerous occasions, the real power behind the throne.
